div.head: INFORMATION FOR WORKING WOMEN.
div.p: INFORMATION FOR WORKING WOMEN.

It is a boast often heard that there are a greater variety of ocrupations open to wmnen now-a-days than ever before. Yet the fact is not wi bout its drawbacks, for women are thus tempted into scores of positions for which they am not titled, with much consequent misery. Thousands of girls, especially in America, sit all day hammering at type-writers and telegraphic instruments, stand tin their feet for a dozen hours at a stretch in shops and storm, and Mud over desks at some sort of writing, till their muscles and heads ache together. In both England and America they labour in fact-nit, long hours over hard and monotonous tasks, often inn fear- fully txrd atmosphere, and for small wages. When they Itniak &Ml] the expense of having physicians, conplisl with other costs of illness, is apt to eonsome their little , savings. 'therefore, any information which will enable • them to lessen such an outgo =lst be welcomed by the hosts of working women. . . . .

div.head: BAZAAR AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: BAZAAR AT LATCHFORD.

A bazaar in aid of the (and for the erection of a parish room in Christ Church Parish, Latchford, was opened in the new Parish Room, on Tuesday after- noon, and continued with great success on Wednes- , day and Thursday. It had been announced that the bazaar would be opened by the Hon. Ellinor Wilson- fatten, but owing to the death of Lund Winmar- grandson that lady was unable to be present, I and Mrs. Charlton Parr performed the ceremony., I I There was a large number of people present at the , opening proceedings, amongst whom were Lady! (Orman, Miss OreenalL the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. M. W. Men. Willis, the Mayoress, I Mrs. Stanton, Mrs, Dun, Canon and Mrs. Greenall, I Mrs. Pickmere, Mr. W. IL Bleck ly, Mr. John Fair- I dough, Mr. O. Dagin, Mrs. Venn, Mrs. Smethurst, I Mrs.J. C. Parr,Mrs. Peter Stubbs, Mrs. Lyon,Mr. and Mrs. Manion, Mrs. Robert Davies, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. William Sharp, Mrs. Wilkinson, the Nev. B. B. Prescott, the Rev. J. M. Prescott, Mrs. W. Tinsley, Mrs. and Miss Long, Mrs. S. Reynolds. the I Rev. J. J. and Mrs. Langham, Mr. and Mrs. Vere Davies, Mrs. and Miss Dodd, Miss Milner, Mr. I Herbert Woods, Mr. and Mrs. S. E. Johnson, the Rev. P. and Mrs. Slater, Mrs. Harrison, Ece. The Rev. B. B. PHESCOTT, Vicar, said that the clergy of the parish and the members of the congregation were grateful Scull who had assisted in getting up the tratimr, and who intended to help in what had been character- ised sea great work. Much had been done, and much, they might say, remained to be done. They mutt not think berms:n, they had had no much help that they : ought to rest and be sattsfigd ; on the contrary, he] thought Swan rather scull to them to put theirshoulders to the wheel to try and rake as moth as they possibly ; could. Ile belissied that about £4OO store was required, and he hoped that those pessent would spend as liberally as they could. Thee all regretted that the Hon. Elinor Wilson-Patten, owing to deep family affliction, was un- able to be present, but he ova., sure she had their deepest sympathy in the heavy bereavement which had fallen upon herself and fussily. Mrs. Parr had kindy contented to open the bazaar, and it was now hit great pleasure to call upon her to do so. 8111` had been with them before to open the first big affair they had five or six years ago, and she was with them again to do another gracious act. After Mrs. Parr had briefly declared the bursar open, the Vicar read the following letter, which 'sad been addressed to Mr. John White by Miss Wilson-Patten : I am sending you a very small contribution of work for your sale, with my sister's parcel. lam sorry that sw- ing to our present sorrow I cannot he present to open Sit.' Istaar. My heartiest good wishes will be with you, because! of the warm sympathy I feel with you and Mr. White in your efforts to do good in your neighbourhood, and because the object of the present effort which you and your neighbours are making seems such an excell- ent one. I believe it is only Whell a parish room is actually built and ready for use that the advantage of it is fully realizesl, and I sincerely hope that you will have a great suet-Amin raising the essetmry funds for the completion of the Latchford parish room." After a vote of thinks had been accorded to Mrs. Parr on tin- proposition of Mr. Coxon, the tale was proceeded with. The following ladies presided at the stalls :—Mrs. Edward Greenal), Mrs. John White, Mrs. Litton, MIN. W"011g, Mrs. John Reynolds, Mrs, John Fairclough, Mrs. Graham, Mm. Dyson, Mrs. Crossley, Mrs. Edits- ten, Mrs. Wallace, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Deacon, and the Misses Fanny Smith, E. Harvey, J. Dun, Litton, Broad- bent, Dunn, Royandt, Reynolds, Fairhurst, Cotton, ; isnsdale, White, J. Litton, F. A. Chappell, Bertha Roberts, Mary Considers, and -Emily ' Cobb. These ladies were very quickly doing a brisk business, in the dispotal of miscellaneous I articles of the description always to be found at haraars. The other attractions,and there were a mod many of them, included, to quote the programme, A Cafe ' CFl:infant, under the mangement and direction of Signor Dwelt:4 Grarnini (Major Douglas Graham), trumpetonajort I the Lands:casts of Sehipkanahl. Bar- men, the greatest showman living, assist.' by Brigadier Sit,' Baron Vtoi e Delstenograph (Mr. Arthur Edelsten), late head ttsk and bottle-washer to the Maharajah of Akker-Spitg Also tits marvellous exhibition of the speaking head, and the mystifying illusion of the Invisi- ble, produced by Rem Joseff Flarremun (Alderman Joseph Harrison). Professor of Thamnaturgy at the Kowan-Tikoarte Kindergarten, together with an art gallery comprising a most interesting collection never public/3.- exhibitetel before, the property of 11. Iturtwoods Esq. (Mr. Herbert Woods.)" Each of these " shows " proved a great meets, and added materially to the Intik of the "takings." There was also a lottery department. The roots had fir the occasion loss very tastefully decorated, ender the supervision of Mr. Arthdrehandley, and the effect was very picturesque.

The. hamar has been a very successful one in every resnoet. tie first by the takings amounted to £302 16s. 311., on the S1.1,1;TICI dav to £93 5.5. 11d., and en the third day to £lO4 10s. 51r1., making a total of £SOQ 12.5. 04.

THE DALSTON TRAGEDY

At rialston, on Sriturday, inquiry was held by Dr. MacDonald, , into the circumstane es:tt tending the loath of Aim Emma South, aged .36, wife of Mr. D. South, of 78. Shnitiland-grove. and their two daughters, Ada, aged 14, and Edith, aged 12. On Wednerilay even- ing Mrs. South murdered her children by beating their heads with a coke hammer,and also cutting their throats, and afterwards committed suicide by cutting her own thririt. The jury returned a verdict that the children ' died from the efts-to of fractures of the skull ; that the injuries were inflicted by thoo mother while temporarily insane; and that while in the same condition she com- mitted suicide.

PRIMITIVE 111 ET FEUDIST DISTRICT CONFERENCE AT EA RLESTOWN. A fraternal meeting and conference of the officiala and members of the Preston Brook, I.ymm, St. Warrington and Widnes, Earlestown and Lowton Circuits of the Primitive Methodist Con- nexion were held in the Primitive Methodist Chapel Legh-st., Earlestown, on Saturday afternoon and evening. There was a large attendance of represen- tatives from each circuit and considerable interest wm manifested in the proceedings. CONN. lONA NSTITIMONS. _ „

..... The afternoon session was opened at half past two, the chair being occupied by the Rev. It. Robinson, resident , minister, and among those presiint were the Rev. W. Evans (Lyn.), Rev. John Dudley (Lowton), Messrs. S. , Owens Widnes), S. Hancock (Parr), E. J. George, T. Or..nd and other gentlemen—The Chairman in an in- troductory address, said that some might object to the I forin or method, bat when's, there was life there must be form. AA method and routine were necessary far their daily lives, so also, were they necessary for their religious life. They wanted inspiration as well as legisla- tion, they wanted fife as well as doctrine, and the great thing they needed, to his mind, was a baptism of fire.— Mr. S. Owens (Widnes), then read a paper on The duty of a church in relation to Connexional institutions:. fle pointed out that duty as a church met them everywhere and he believed the greatest amount of good could be I accomplished by denominationalism. They must ! first he true to their own society, and give their moral and material support to the circle of which I they formed a part. He alluded to the Sunday School Union asan important institution and spoke of its modern ! development tie pointed out other agencies and societies : in connection with the church and Said they all claimed their hearty sympathy and support.—Mr. E. J. George 1 (Farlestown) opened the dioassion, and referred to the connesional hook departm at, commending the work of the connexional editor and his agents.—The Rev. J. 1 Dudley (Lowton) referred to the goml work of Sunday schools, and said he thought their libraries should be replenished with connexional literature. The Dago' light and frivolous literature of the day should be substituted by goml books which could be put into the hands of young people.—The Rev. W. Evans (Lymm), : said that any disloyalty always grieved him. He coin- minded the district evangelistic scheme and thought it should be supported, as it was a gnat improvement on : former methods. Ile spoke of the excellency of their reward books and hoped the book-room establislunent would he more generally patronised.—Mr. Hancock, ! (Parr) spoke of the good he had received by his attend- anoe at such mini erences.—The Chairman referred toasi institution about to be launched for helping their over- burdened chapels and hoped the maple would not be backward in supporting the scheme . A vote of thanks was tendered tithe essayist on the motion of Mr. Gyton (Preston Brook), seconded by Mr. Austin (Earlestown), and the company adjourned for tea. EVENING MEETING. The tea was served in the sehoolroom and a goodly number of persons sat down. At half-past seven a meet- ing was held in the chapel and was largely attended. Mr. T. Ormand, of Earlestown, occupied the chair, and was supported by the ministers named. The ('hainnan , gave a brief address, and the H.v. IV. Evans (Lyinm), spoke on The weakness .'fib. church and the sources of her strength." He urged the benefit of prayers coi- -1 lectively as a church and odd what was necemary for them as a church, was necessary h'e them as indivi- : duals. The thee. J. Dudley (Lov-ton) read a paper !on " Woman's work is the Church." He pro- ceeded to point out that women could don grand and good work in her home influence: that by tier tenderness and sympathy she was eminently fitted to visit the afflicted, the needy and the sorrowing, that Iby her patience and winsomeness she could play an important part in the training of the young for God. The Rev. It. Robinson next raid a paper on "Gambling —its evil and the necessity for energetic action on the part of Churches and Sunday schools to .iintoract it." He advised all young men to atotain from gambling as ! it lead to beggary, to forgery, to robbery and saicide. He quoted from a periodical sn lotteries at bantam and , asked t. 11.111 to their hands be clean in that niatter hnd : have nothing to do with gambling in the church. Votes of thanks were tendenid to the speakers, and the meeting concluded with singing 311.1 prayer.

div.p: EXCITEMENT UNABATED.
BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

STEALING A FLITCH OF BACON. On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, two men named John Baekbote.e and William Mien, butchers, pleaded guilty to having stolen a flitch of , bacon, value 100., from a shop in the Market-shed kept by William OW, butcher, Bridget. They wore each tined 400. and costs, or a month's imprisonment in default of payment. A DISHONEST WORICSIAN. Joseph Bate, parlor, Itllesmere-st., was fined '2Als. and costs by the Warrington magistrates on Mon- day for having stolen a pick antis -made, value 45., belonging to another pastor named Renwick. Prisoner was temporarily employed during the absence of Renwick throut.h illness, and took away the tools on the completion of his work. THEFT OF A FERRET AT ORFORD. On Wednesday morning, at the Warrington ' County Petty Sessions, a young man named Joseph Ellison was charged with having stolen a canvas bag and a ferret, of the value of lb.. the property of William Jackson, son of a farmer at Orford. Prisoner bad been working at the farm, and it WLS alleged that he took the ferret and sold it for 4s. lb o ploadrd guilty, and was tined 10s, and costs, or 11 days' imprisonment
